title: Al-Qurtubi's commentary
hook: the Andalusian commentator focused on law
tomorrow: two good options, one choice. how do you weigh it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ibn Kathir: the book explains itself, Qur'an by Qur'an first. Today, a commentator who reads it for the rules hidden in plain sight.

Every restaurant restroom has the sign: employees must wash hands. Simple, until somebody asks: how long, up to where, does a quick rinse count? The Qur'an has a hand-washing verse too: "O ye who believe! When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows." It goes on: wipe your heads, wash your feet to the ankles. That's the washing before prayer, wudu. Short and clear. Then a scholar from Cordoba, in Muslim Spain, sat down with it, and found a page of law inside.
screen: `EMPLOYEES MUST WASH HANDS.` → `THE VERSE: WASH, UP TO THE ELBOWS.` → `A PAGE OF LAW INSIDE.`

segments.voice: That scholar is al-Qurtubi, and his commentary is called the Collection of the Qur'an's Rulings. He reads verses for what they ask people to do, and he asks the questions a body asks at the sink. Does "up to the elbows" include the elbows, or stop just short? Does the washing need an intention behind it, or is wet enough? How much of the head is wiped? Here the schools of law split: Imam Malik, whose school al-Qurtubi followed, says the whole head; al-Shafi'i says part of it is enough. Al-Qurtubi gives his own school's view and lays out the others with their reasons. Even the feet carry a question. The Arabic has two recognized readings at that word, and they point different ways: Sunni schools wash the feet; Shia jurists wipe them. One vowel, two practices, each with its own careful reasoning. Here's the thing worth repeating tonight: one short verse about washing up holds a page of law, and scholars who differ over it are each trying to obey it. Law in the verses, all the way down to the elbow.
screen: `THE COLLECTION OF RULINGS.` · `UP TO, OR INCLUDING, THE ELBOWS?` · `WHOLE HEAD OR PART: SCHOOLS DIFFER.` · `TWO READINGS AT THE FEET.` · then, large: `LAW IN THE VERSES.`

segments.voice: If there's water near you, wash your hands slowly, up to the wrists or to the elbows, feeling the water at each part. If not, run one palm slowly over the back of the other hand and up the forearm, as if washing. Let each part get your full attention, one at a time, as the verse names them.
screen: `WATER, OR AN EMPTY PALM.` · `HAND, WRIST, FOREARM.` · `ONE PART AT A TIME.`
